title: hjkl and word motions
summary: Move by character and by word, and know exactly where w, b and e land.

steps.title: Hands on the home row
body: `h` left, `j` down (j hangs below the line), `k` up, `l` right. Arrow keys work too, but `hjkl` keeps your fingers on the home row, and every other motion builds on the same idea: **a motion is a key that moves the cursor**. Later, an operator in front of a motion acts on the text it moves over (`d` + `w` = delete a word).
> **Practise:** open **Labs → Vim & nano trainer** and run this lesson's challenges until the keys come without thinking.

steps.prompt: Match the key to the direction.

steps.title: Words and WORDS
body: vim has two definitions of a word:
- a **word** is a run of letters, digits and `_`, **or** a run of other punctuation. `foo.bar(1)` is the words `foo` `.` `bar` `(` `1` `)`.
- a **WORD** is any run of non-blank characters. `foo.bar(1)` is one WORD.
| `w` / `W` | start of the next word / WORD |
| `b` / `B` | start of the current or previous word / WORD |
| `e` / `E` | end of the current or next word / WORD |
Lowercase is precise inside code; uppercase skips over punctuation-heavy things like paths and URLs in one jump.

steps.prompt: The line is `cfg.load(path)` and the cursor is on the `c`. You press `w` once. Which character is the cursor on?
steps.explain: `cfg` is a word of letters; `.` is punctuation, so it is the next word.

steps.prompt: Same line, `cfg.load(path)`, cursor on `c`, and it is the last line of the file. You press `W` once. Which character is the cursor on?
steps.explain: The whole line is one WORD, so there is no next WORD. On the last line of a file vim moves to the last character instead.

steps.prompt: The line is `rm -rf /var/tmp/build` with the cursor on `r` of `rm`. How many presses of `W` reach the `/` of `/var`?
Is it one word or several? (lowercase `w` definition)
steps.explain: `==` is one run of punctuation, so it is a single word. `x2` and `max_value` are letters, digits and `_`.

steps.title: Where does w land?
prompt: Write `int W(string line, int col)` that returns the column `w` moves to, staying on one line:
- characters are of three kinds: blank (whitespace), keyword (letter, digit or `_`), other (punctuation).
- from `col`, skip the rest of the current run of the same kind (if it is not blank), then skip blanks.
- if that runs off the end of the line, return `line.Length - 1` (the last character).
solution: if (k != 0) while (i < n && Kind(line[i]) == k) i++;
hints: Skip characters while `Kind` is the same as the starting one, then skip blanks.
Do not skip anything in the first loop when you start on a blank.
template: Dojo.Eq("from the middle of a word", 6, W("hello world", 2));
Dojo.Eq("double punctuation is one word", 5, W("a == b", 2));
Dojo.Eq("last word stays on the line", 10, W("hello world", 8));

steps.title: Where do b and e land?
prompt: Now write `int E(string line, int col)` and `int B(string line, int col)` using the same three kinds:
- `E`: move one character right, skip blanks, then move to the **last** character of that run. If you run off the end, return `line.Length - 1`.
- `B`: move one character left, skip blanks going left, then move to the **first** character of that run. If you run off the start, return 0.
`E("hello world", 0)` is 4; `E("hello world", 4)` is 10; `B("hello world", 6)` is 0; `B("hello world", 8)` is 6.
hints: Both start by moving one step, then skip blanks.
Then extend while the neighbour has the same `Kind`.
template: Dojo.Eq("e to end of first word", 4, E("hello world", 0));
Dojo.Eq("e from a word end jumps to the next end", 10, E("hello world", 4));
Dojo.Eq("e on a one-character run", 3, E("cfg.load", 2));
Dojo.Eq("b from the start of a word", 0, B("hello world", 6));
Dojo.Eq("b from inside a word", 6, B("hello world", 8));
